'''''Solanum carolinense''''', the '''Carolina horsenettle''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SOCA3|taxon=Solanum carolinense|accessdate=17 November 2015}}</ref> is not a [[Urtica|true nettle]], but a member of the [[Solanaceae]], or [[nightshade]] family. It is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] herbaceous plant, native to the southeastern United States, though its range has expanded throughout much of temperate North America.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://plants.usda.gov/home/plantProfile?symbol=soca3 | title=USDA Plants Database }}</ref> The plant is considered to be [[Invasive species|invasive]] in parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and Australia.<ref>{{Cite web |title=EPPO Panel on Invasive Alien Plants |url=https://www.eppo.int/MEETINGS/2022_meetings/https%3A%2F%2Fwww.eppo.int%2FMEETINGS%2F2022_meetings%2Fp_iap |access-date=2025-10-17 |website=www.eppo.int |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Solanum carolinense [Morella della Carolina] - Flora Italiana |url=http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=solanum+carolinense |access-date=2025-10-17 |website=luirig.altervista.org}}</ref> The stem and undersides of larger leaf veins are covered with [[Thorns, spines, and prickles|prickles]].

"Horsenettle" is also written "horse nettle" or "horse-nettle", though [[USDA]] publications usually use the one-word form. Though there are other horsenettle nightshades, ''S. carolinense'' is the species most commonly called ''"the'' horsenettle". Other common names include '''radical weed, sand brier or briar, [[bull nettle]], tread-softly, [[Solanum mammosum]] ("apple of Sodom"), devil's tomato '''and''' [[wild tomato]].'''{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

==Description==
[[File:Solanum carolinense L. Carolina horsenettle.tiff|thumb|Illustration of Carolina Horsenettle from a 1913 field guide]]
[[File:Horsenettle1846.JPG|thumb|Flowers]]

The leaves are [[Leaf shape|alternate, elliptic-oblong to oval]], {{convert|2+1/2|to|4+1/2|in|cm|0|order=flip|abbr=off}} long, and each is irregularly lobed or coarsely toothed. Both surfaces are covered with fine hairs. The leaves smell like potatoes when crushed. The flowers have five petals and are usually white or purple with yellow centers, though there is a blue variant that resembles the tomato flower. The fruits are [[Berry (botany)|berries]] that resemble tomatoes. The immature fruit is dark green with light green stripes, turning yellow and wrinkled as it matures. Each fruit contains around 60 seeds. It flowers throughout the summer, from April to October (in the northern hemisphere). The plant grows to {{convert|3|ft|cm|-1|order=flip|abbr=on}} tall, is [[Perennial plant|perennial]], and spreads by both seeds and underground [[rhizome]]. Stems of older plants are woody.<ref name="bradley">{{cite web|title=Identification and Control of Horsenettle ''(Solanum carolinense)'' in Virginia|url=http://www.ppws.vt.edu/scott/weed_id/horsenettle.PDF|access-date=6 October 2013|last1=Bradley|first1=Kevin W.|last2=Hagood|first2=Edward S.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100612155538/http://www.ppws.vt.edu/scott/weed_id/horsenettle.PDF|archive-date=2010-06-12|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
Many parts of the plant have historically been used to create medicines to treat various conditions. It was listed in [[United States Pharmacopeia|the United States National Formulary]] from 1916 to 1936 for use by pharmacists.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Solanum carolinense (Apple of Sodom, Bull Nettle, Carolina Horse-Nettle, Devil's Potato, Devil's Tomato, Horsenettle, Horse Nettle, Poisonous Potato, Thorn Apple, Wild Tomato) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/solanum-carolinense/ |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref><ref name="georgetown-medical">{{Cite web |title=URBAN HERBS: Horse Nettle |url=http://pharmacology.georgetown.edu:80/urbanherbs/horse_nettle.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130329102805/http://pharmacology.georgetown.edu:80/urbanherbs/horse_nettle.htm |archive-date=2013-03-29 |access-date=2025-10-17 |website=pharmacology.georgetown.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Solanum carolinense - Useful Temperate Plants |url=https://temperate.theferns.info/plant/Solanum+carolinense |access-date=2023-09-20 |website=temperate.theferns.info}}</ref> However all parts of the plant, including its tomato-like fruit, contain toxins in varying degrees due to the presence of [[solanine]] [[glycoalkaloid]]s which is a toxic [[alkaloid]] and one of the plant's natural defenses. While ingesting any part of the plant can cause fever, headache, scratchy throat, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, ingesting the fruit can cause abdominal pain, circulatory and respiratory depression, or even death.<ref name="georgetown-medical" />

==Ecology==

===Habitat===
''Solanum carolinense'' can be found growing in pastures, roadsides, railroad margins, and in [[Disturbance (ecology)|disturbed areas]] and waste ground. They can grow to about {{cvt|1|m|ftin}} tall, but are typically shorter, existing as [[subshrubs]].<ref name="bradley" /> They prefer full sun, and can tolerate both wet or dry conditions. They grow readily in sandy or [[loam]]y soils, and may also tolerate a wide range of soil types. They are most vigorous and most likely to become weedy or aggressive on disturbed sites, but can also be found in less disturbed habitats.<ref name="illinois">{{Cite web |title=Horse Nettle (Solanum carolinense) |url=http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/prairie/plantx/hrs_nettlex.htm |access-date=2025-10-17 |website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info}}</ref>

===Faunal associations and diseases===
Bumble bees pollinate the flowers of ''Solanum carolinense''.

At least thirty-two insects, as well as the meadow vole ''[[Microtus pennsylvanicus]]'', have been recorded feeding on this species in [[Virginia]] alone.<ref name="wise">{{Cite journal |last=Wise |first=Michael J. |year=2007 |title=The Herbivores of Solanum carolinense (Horsenettle) in Northern Virginia: Natural History and Damage Assessment |url=http://www.bioone.org/doi/abs/10.1656/1528-7092%282007%296%5B505%3ATHOSCH%5D2.0.CO%3B2 |journal=Southeastern Naturalist |language=en |volume=6 |issue=3 |pages=505–522 |doi=10.1656/1528-7092(2007)6[505:THOSCH]2.0.CO;2 |issn=1528-7092}}</ref>  The caterpillars of the ''[[Synanthedon rileyana]]'' moth<ref name="illinois" /> and the ''[[Manduca sexta]]'' (tobacco hornworm) moth feed on the plant.  ''Manduca sexta'' moths prefer inbred plants to outbred plants. ''[[Leptinotarsa juncta]]'' (the false potato beetle) specializes on this plant, and ''[[Epitrix fuscula]]'' (the eggplant flea beetle) eats it as well.<ref name="twospecialists">{{Cite journal |last=Wise |first=Michael J. |last2=Sacchi |first2=Christopher F. |date=1996-10-01 |title=Impact of two specialist insect herbivores on reproduction of horse nettle, Solanum carolinense |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00334658 |journal=Oecologia |language=en |volume=108 |issue=2 |pages=328–337 |doi=10.1007/BF00334658 |issn=1432-1939}}</ref>  These two beetles are its two primary [[herbivores]], and can reduce fruit production by as much as 75% relative to plants protected from all insects.<ref name="twospecialists" />  ''[[Anthonomus nigrinus]]'' (the potato bud weevil) feeds on the flowers, and ''[[Trichobaris trinotata]]'' (the potato stalk borer) bores into the stems.<ref name="wise" />  This plant is also eaten by ''[[Leptinotarsa decemlineata]]'' (the Colorado potato beetle) and has been recorded as being eaten at very low rates by [[pupae]] of an unidentified species of the family [[Gelechiidae]].<ref name="weedscience">{{Cite journal |last=Nichols |first=Robert L. |last2=Cardina |first2=John |last3=Lynch |first3=Robert L. |last4=Minton |first4=Norman A. |last5=Wells |first5=Homer D. |date=1992 |title=Insects, Nematodes, and Pathogens Associated with Horsenettle (Solanum carolinense) in Bermudagrass (Cynodon dactylon) Pastures |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4045349 |journal=Weed Science |volume=40 |issue=2 |pages=320–325 |doi=10.2307/4045349?uid=3739864&uid=2129&uid=2&uid=70&uid=4&uid=3739256&sid=21104146694647 |issn=0043-1745}}</ref>
[[File:Milkweed_leaf_beete_on_horseNettle.webm|thumb|center|False potato beetle larvae consuming horsenettle. The leaves contain embedded leaf  prickles that extend through the leaf  protecting it from many herbivores. ]]

Parasitic [[nematodes]] of the genus ''[[Pratylenchus]]'' have been found on [[lesions]] on its roots, however causing little damage. The fungus ''[[Rhizoctonia solani]]'' was found causing [[root rot]], particularly under wet conditions in plants damaged by trampling.<ref name="weedscience" /> The plant is also affected by [[Erysiphaceae|powdery mildew]] species such as ''{{ill|Podosphaera solanacearum|ceb}}''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Braun |first=Uwe |title=Taxonomic manual of the Erysiphales (powdery mildews) |last2=Cook |first2=Roger T. A. |date=2012 |publisher=CBS-KNAW fungal biodiversity centre |isbn=978-90-70351-89-2 |series=CBS biodiversity series |location=Utrecht}}</ref>

Fruits are eaten by a variety of native animals, including [[ring-necked pheasant]], [[bobwhite]], [[wild turkey]], and [[striped skunk]]. Most mammals avoid eating the stems and leaves due to both the spines and toxicity of the plant.<ref name="illinois" />

==Weed==
Carolina horsenettle is considered a [[noxious weed]] in one US state (Alaska).<ref>{{Cite web | url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=soca3 | title=Plants Profile for Solanum carolinense (Carolina horsenettle)}}</ref> It can spread [[Vegetative reproduction|vegetative]]ly by underground [[rhizome]]s as well as by seed. It is resistant to many postemergent [[herbicide]]s and somewhat resistant to [[broad-spectrum]] [[herbicides]] such as [[glyphosate]] and [[2,4-D]]. In fact, herbicide use often selects for horsenettle by removing competing weeds. It is an especially despised weed by gardeners who hand-weed, as the prickles tend to penetrate the skin and then break off when the plant is grasped. The deep root also makes it difficult to remove.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}
